extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying formal/first-order logic and proof theory
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, axioms, inference rules, and metatheorems for axiomatic (Hilbert/Frege) derivations in propositional and first-order logic; includes Henkin expansion and the completeness theorem outline and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (axiomatic derivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation from Γ is a finite sequence α1, ..., αn of wffs where for each i one of: (1) αi ∈ Γ; (2) αi is an axiom; or (3) αi follows from one or more earlier αj's by a rule of inference. A derivation 'derives' its last wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 100A. The text emphasizes that what counts as a correct derivation depends on which inference rules and axioms are allowed; to show Γ ⊢ α one must exhibit (or argue for existence of) such a finite sequence ending in α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of inference (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of inference gives a sufficient condition for what counts as a correct inference step in a derivation from Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 100B. Rules may be simple (e.g., 'if α ∈ Γ then α is always a correct inference step') or may appeal to earlier wffs in the derivation. Concrete instances include modus ponens and the quantifier rules (qr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens (mp)
rubrics_metrics.description: If β → α and β occur earlier in the derivation, then α is a correct inference step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 101B (abbreviated 'mp'). The text shows how mp functions as the single rule in many Hilbert-style systems and illustrates its use in multiple example derivations (e.g., deriving (¬δ ∨ φ) → (δ → φ)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms for propositional connectives (Ax0)
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom schemas for propositional connectives comprise all instances of the listed forms (eqs. (10.1)–(10.14)): (α ∧ β) → α; (α ∧ β) → β; α → (β → (α ∧ β)); α → (α ∨ β); α → (β ∨ α); (α → γ) → ((β → γ) → ((α ∨ β) → γ)); α → (β → α); (α → (β → γ)) → ((α → β) → (α → γ)); (α → β) → ((α → ¬β) → ¬α); ¬α → (α → β); ⊤; ⊥ → α; (α → ⊥) → ¬α; ¬¬α → α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 101A. These schemas are the logical axioms from which many propositional facts are derived via mp; examples in the text show how particular instances of these axioms are chosen to drive derivations (e.g., using eq. (10.6), (10.7), (10.8), (10.10) in constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifier axioms are all instances of: ∀x β → β(t) and β(t) → ∃x β, for any closed term t (eqs. (10.15) and (10.16)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 102A. These axioms connect quantified formulas to their instances; when combined with quantifier rules they allow introduction/elimination of quantifiers in derivations (careful about 't' being free-for-x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for quantifiers (qr)
rubrics_metrics.description: If β → α(a) occurs in the derivation and a does not occur in Γ or β, then β → ∀x α(x) is a correct inference step. If α(a) → β occurs and a does not occur in Γ or β, then ∃x α(x) → β is a correct inference step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 102B. Abbreviated 'qr'. The rules include an eigenvariable condition: the introduced constant a must not occur in Γ or the wff being generalized. These rules are used in later proofs, especially in the Deduction Theorems with quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability and theorem notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ⊢ α means there is a derivation from Γ ending in α. A wff α is a theorem if ⊢ α (i.e., derivable from the empty set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions 100C/100D and reiterated in 105A/105B. The text uses these notations throughout; many propositions are statements about when ⊢ or Γ ⊢ hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (proof-theoretic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of wffs is consistent iff Γ ⊬ ⊥; it is inconsistent otherwise. Γ is inconsistent iff Γ ⊢ α for every α (Proposition 105G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 105C and Proposition 105G (exercise). Consistency here is syntactic: absence of a derivation of contradiction. The text uses consistency as the central hypothesis in the completeness construction (extend to a saturated/complete consistent set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexivity, Monotonicity, Transitivity of ⊢
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflexivity: if α ∈ Γ then Γ ⊢ α. Monotonicity: if Γ ⊆ Δ and Γ ⊢ α then Δ ⊢ α. Transitivity: if Γ ⊢ α and {α} ∪ Δ ⊢ β then Γ ∪ Δ ⊢ β (Propositions 105D–105F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These basic structural properties are used repeatedly (e.g., concatenating derivations to combine proofs; see proofs of Prop. 105F and uses in later propositions and theorems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness (proof-theoretic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) If Γ ⊢ α then there is a finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ such that Γ0 ⊢ α. 2) If every finite subset of Γ is consistent, then Γ is consistent (Proposition 105H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 105H. The text notes this follows because derivations are finite and hence only depend on finitely many premises; compactness is also a semantic consequence of completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-modus ponens (Proposition 106A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ α and Γ ⊢ α → β then Γ ⊢ β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a 'meta' version of MP in proofs about derivability. The short formal derivation is given (Hyp: α; Hyp: α→β; then β by MP) and combined with Prop.105F to conclude Γ ⊢ β.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction Theorem (propositional, Theorem 106B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ∪ {α} ⊢ β iff Γ ⊢ α → β. If Γ ⊢ α → β then also Γ ∪ {α} ⊢ β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 106B. Proof by induction on the length of derivations from Γ ∪ {α}; relies on chosen axiom schemas (notably eqs. (10.7) and (10.8)) so that the theorem holds. Examples show derivation of α→α used in base case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction Theorem with quantifiers (Theorem 107A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ∪ {α} ⊢ β then Γ ⊢ α → β (the version accommodating quantifier rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 107A. The inductive proof deals with cases where the last inference is qr, using eigenvariable conditions and auxiliary implications; requires additional lemmas about instances and qr to move quantifier reasoning 'outside' the assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived logical facts (ex falso, double negation, contraposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of derivable metatheorems: e.g., {α, ¬α} ⊢ β (Explosion/Ex Falso), {¬¬α} ⊢ α (Double Negation Elimination), contraposition properties, and transitivity of implication (Proposition 106C items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 106C lists these useful consequences that follow from the axiom schemas and MP; they are invoked in many subsequent derivations and metatheoretical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositional connective derivability properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts such as α ∧ β ⊢ α and α ∧ β ⊢ β; α, β ⊢ α ∧ β; α ∨ β, ¬α, ¬β is inconsistent; α ⊢ α ∨ β and β ⊢ α ∨ β; α, α → β ⊢ β (Propositions 109A–109C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are proven from the axiom schemas (notably eqs. (10.1)–(10.6)) and mp; the text provides short derivations to illustrate how to manipulate conjunctions, disjunctions, and implications in the axiomatic system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier derivability facts
rubrics_metrics.description: If c is a fresh constant symbol not occurring in Γ or α(x) and Γ ⊢ α(c), then Γ ⊢ ∀x α(x) (Theorem 1010A). Also, ∀x α(x) ⊢ α(t) (Proposition 1010B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results rely on the quantifier axioms and the Deduction Theorem; the freshness/eigenvariable condition is essential when using a closed term 'c' to generalize to ∀x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of the derivation system
rubrics_metrics.description: All axioms are valid in every structure and if Γ ⊢ α then Γ ⊨ α (Theorem 1011B). Consequence corollaries: if ⊢ α then α is valid; if Γ is satisfiable then it is consistent (Corollary 1011D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 1011A verifies validity of axioms (example given for eq. (10.15)); Theorem 1011B proves soundness by induction on derivation length, treating cases for mp and qr. Soundness is the 'safety' guarantee: the system doesn't prove semantically false sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and rules for equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Add axiom schemas t = t and t1 = t2 → (β(t1) → β(t2)) for closed terms t, t1, t2 (eqs. (10.17)–(10.18)). Consequences: Γ ⊢ t = t and substitutivity results (Propositions 1012B–1012D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 1012A. These axioms incorporate the predicate '=' into the axiomatic derivations; Prop.1012D shows how equality plus instance derivability yields substitution of equals in derivations via two applications of mp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete set (definition) and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of sentences is complete iff for any sentence α, either α ∈ Γ or ¬α ∈ Γ (Definition 112A). For complete consistent Γ: if Γ ⊢ α then α ∈ Γ; α → β ∈ Γ iff either α ∉ Γ or β ∈ Γ (Proposition 112B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete consistent sets 'decide' every sentence and play a central role in model construction: from a complete consistent Γ (in an expanded language) one defines a structure by reading off which atomic sentences belong to Γ; completeness of Γ ensures no atomic truth-values are left undecided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henkin expansion and saturated set
rubrics_metrics.description: Henkin trick: expand language by countably many new constants di and for each 1-free wff α(x) add a sentence δn := ¬∀x α(x) → ¬α(cn) where cn is a new constant chosen fresh for α. A set Γ is saturated iff for each α(x) there is a constant c with ¬∀x α(x) → ¬α(c) ∈ Γ (Definition 113B–113C). Lemma 113D: every consistent Γ can be extended to a saturated consistent Γ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction picks fresh constants to witness existential counterexamples for false universal sentences; the lemma proves consistency is preserved in the expansion by induction on adding δn, relying on eigenvariable choices (cn not appearing earlier). This is preparatory to building term-models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term model construction (outline) / treatment of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a model A(Γ*) whose domain is (initially) the set of closed terms, interpret predicate symbols by which atomic sentences are in Γ*, and interpret function symbols by syntactic term-formation; to handle = one uses equivalence classes or sets of terms identifying those the theory requires to be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §11.1 outlines: if terms are taken as domain, then t = t' is true only when terms coincide; to make nontrivial equalities true (e.g., (0+0)=0), the construction uses sets/equivalence classes of terms determined by Γ* so that all terms the theory equates share the same interpretation. Later definitions/lemmas (Definitions 115A, 116D, Lemmas 115D, 116G referenced) show |=A(Γ*) α iff α ∈ Γ*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness theorem (two equivalent formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: First formulation: if Γ ⊨ α then Γ ⊢ α (semantic consequence implies provability). Second formulation (model-existence): every consistent set of sentences is satisfiable. These formulations are equivalent and imply compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem consequences (§11.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction and outline discuss strategy: extend a consistent Γ to a saturated, complete, consistent Γ*, then build a term-model A(Γ*) and show it satisfies Γ*; completeness follows. The text emphasizes the equivalence of the semantic and syntactic statements and some corollaries (compactness, existence of countable models).
